In the previous chapter, we used the normal distribution to determine the probability of seeing individual scores within a given range. But researchers usually collect a sample and summarize its scores with a statistic, like the mean. In Chapter 4, we saw that sample means vary because of sampling error, even though their errors balance out in the long run. Now we'll ask how widely those means vary, and which results would be surprising.

## The Quincunx

Before we proceed, take a moment to enjoy this little toy. (It's a digital version of a real thing you can buy and keep on your desk to turn to in moments of boredom.)

## The Quincunx

{{< interactive-figure

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Let them fall" data-action='{"drop":0,"show-expected":false}' data-repeat-action='{"run":"next","drop":400,"show-expected":false}' data-repeat-label="Replay"}
Click Replay to start. Try it a couple of times: what changes, and what stays similar?
:::
::::

:::::

It's called a Galton board, after Francis Galton, who developed it in the 1870s. (Galton also called it the Quincunx, meaning five points, as in the arrangement of groups of pegs.) The physical version is a little box with a clear front, rows of pegs, and lots of little balls (originally lead shot, like from shotgun pellets; ammunition manufacturers by this time were able to make the precise, uniform spheres that the demonstration requires).

As Galton inscribed on the original device, when set upright on a level table, "the shot will all drop into the funnel, and running thence through its mouth, will pursue devious courses through the harrow and will accumulate in the vertical compartments at the bottom, there affording a representation of the law of dispersion."

![The original Quincunx, commissioned by Galton and made by scientific instrument manufacturers Tisley & Spiller in 1873. © 2017 University College London, CC BY-NC-SA](resources/figures/quincunx.jpeg){#fig-quincunx}

By "law of dispersion," Galton meant the tendency for the balls to end up in a predictable distribution---this is the same approximation of the normal distribution that Abraham de Moivre had discovered by thinking about a random process like flipping a coin many times. Each individual ball's course is unpredictable, but the aggregate of all those “devious courses” looks roughly the same each time.^[The exact distribution is binomial; the normal curve approximates its shape, just as in de Moivre's coin-toss example in Chapter 6.]

In our digital board, each ball encounters twelve pegs, with an independent 50/50 chance of bouncing left or right at each one. To end up in the far-left slot, it has to bounce left every time. There is only one way for that to happen, just like there's only one way to roll two dice and get a total of two. To land in the middle, a ball needs to take six lefts and six rights, and there are *many* different sequences that produce that mix, just like there are many ways to roll a seven with the pair of dice. We can't predict any one ball's path, but we can describe the pattern of possible landing places.

## Sampling Error

Our purpose in this chapter is to understand how sampling from a population works---how we can quantify our trust in a sample as a fair representation of the population it came from. The Quincunx is a nice visual analogy for that process. Imagine that each ball is collecting a sample as it falls through the pegs. Each bounce supplies one observation; the final slot is the sample statistic, summarizing all twelve observations.

Let's make the analogy more concrete by comparing the Quincunx to political opinion polling. Say two candidates are running for office, candidate Left and candidate Right. In the population, support for the two candidates is exactly split, 50/50. If we select twelve people at random and ask which candidate they prefer, we might expect to find that half of the people in our sample support each candidate. But because of the kind of sampling error we encountered in Chapter 4, the proportion in our sample need not be exactly 50/50. It wouldn't be too surprising if we ended up with seven supporters of Candidate Left and only five of Candidate Right. Or even 8 and 4. In fact, there is a chance that we could randomly end up with 12 people who all support Candidate Left. It's relatively unlikely, but not out of the question. This is like one of the Quincunx balls bouncing left twelve times in a row and ending up in the far-left slot. Repeat the poll over and over with different samples of 12 people and the results would form a distribution like the pile on the board. Results near 50% support for Candidate Left would be common, while results near 0% or 100% would be rare.

What if we had a sample of 100 people, rather than 12? In this case we'd expect something like 50 people to support each candidate, but it wouldn't be too surprising if we saw something like 60/40. It *would* be surprising if we happened to get 100 people who all support Candidate Left. Now what if our sample size was 1,000? Or 1,000,000? Your intuition is probably telling you that the larger the sample, the more surprising an extremely lop-sided result would be.

This is, in effect, what the error bars on graphs of opinion poll results convey. (The precise math behind the margin of error is something we'll talk more about in Chapter 10.) @fig-election-poll shows the results of two different polls conducted shortly before the 2000 U.S. presidential election, showing people's support for the two main candidates, George W. Bush and Al Gore (support for other candidates was also surveyed, but their shares are not shown here). The error bars show the range of results that would be expected from repeated samples of the same size, assuming that the poll was conducted fairly and that the sample was representative of the population.

::: {#fig-election-poll}

{{< interactive-figure electionPoll makeGraph options='{"type":"interval","data":[{"label":"Bush (Pew)","estimate":49,"lower":46,"upper":52,"color":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)"},{"label":"Bush (Reuters/MSNBC)","estimate":46,"lower":43.2,"upper":48.8,"color":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)"},{"label":"Gore (Pew)","estimate":47,"lower":44,"upper":50,"color":"var(--graph-series-1, #0072b2)"},{"label":"Gore (Reuters/MSNBC)","estimate":48,"lower":45.2,"upper":50.8,"color":"var(--graph-series-1, #0072b2)"}],"scale":"percent","width":640,"height":360,"maxWidth":"640px","labels":{"x":"Estimated popular vote share"},"animate":false,"orientation":"horizontal","xDomain":[41,55],"ariaLabel":"Two final pre-election polls from November 2000. Reuters/MSNBC/Zogby (about 1,200 likely voters): Bush 46%, Gore 48%, plus or minus about 2.8 percentage points."}' fallback="Pew: Bush 49% (46% to 52%), Gore 47% (44% to 50%). Two final pre-election polls' estimates of the popular vote in November 2000. Pew's survey of 1,301 likely voters put Bush ahead, 49% to 47%, with a reported sampling margin of ±3 percentage points; Reuters/MSNBC's tracking poll (conducted by Zogby, roughly 1,200 likely voters) put Gore ahead instead, 48% to 46%, with an implied sampling margin of about ±2.8 percentage points. Only the two leading candidates are shown. Sources: [Pew Research Center, November 2–5, 2000](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2000/11/06/popular-vote-a-tossup-bush-49-gore-47-nader-4/); Reuters/MSNBC figures as tabulated in @walsh2009lies.^[Before allocating undecided voters, Pew had Bush at 45%, Gore 43%, Nader 4%, Buchanan less than 1%, and 8% undecided; the headline estimates shown here allocate those undecided voters. The Pew bars use the [published sampling margin](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2000/11/06/methodology-169/). Reuters/MSNBC did not publish a margin of error alongside this figure; the ±2.8 points shown is calculated from the poll's approximate sample size the same way Pew's is. Neither poll's bars include uncertainty from allocating undecided voters or subsequent changes in voting intentions.]

:::

Notice that Bush's error bars across the two separate polls overlap, as do Gore's, meaning that the polls are not in conflict with each other; even though the exact proportions are different, they are within the same margin of error. Bush and Gore's error bars also overlap, meaning the sampling uncertainty was larger than the gap between the candidates. The Pew report of the result noted that "the contest is so close that we cannot confidently predict the winner of the popular vote."

The result of the actual vote, conducted a couple of days later, was that 47.9% of the popular vote went to Bush and 48.4% to Gore, both within the margin of error of these polls---but Bush won the Electoral College after the Supreme Court halted the Florida recount. As we've seen, real life is often messier than idealized numbers: sampling variability, people changing their minds or withholding opinions, and the workings of electoral systems all complicate what a poll can tell us about what will happen.

### Sampling Error with IQ Scores

The opinion poll results summarize categorical responses with a proportion. Now we'll turn to quantitative data. What would happen if we could repeatedly take samples from a population and summarize each sample with a quantitative statistic like the mean?

Say we have a population of people with normally distributed IQ scores, with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 (a kind of transformed distribution we mentioned in Chapter 5). We randomly collect ten observations and find their mean. Then we draw another ten and repeat. This is effectively the same thing we did in @act-tracking-bias in Chapter 4, but there we focused on bias: as we collected more samples, we tracked their individual errors---the difference between the sample mean and the true population mean---and then averaged all the errors to see how the errors for the unbiased statistics approached zero. This time we'll collect the sample means themselves (not their errors) into a block histogram, so we can see which means occur most often and what their distribution looks like as they pile up.

::::: {#act-sampling-iq .callout-tip .interactive .no-controls}
## Build the sampling distribution

{{< interactive-figure iqSamplingDistribution makeSamplingPathway options='{"seed":"iq-sampling-distribution-v1","mean":100,"sd":15,"sampleSize":10,"sampleCount":200,"binWidth":1,"xlim":[70,130],"populationMarkers":340,"populationAxisLabel":"IQ score","sampleAxis":true,"sampleMeanStyle":"block","showPopulationAxisLabel":true,"showSampleAxisLabel":false,"showDistributionAxisLabel":false,"fallObservationsOnRepeat":false,"repeatInterval":240,"showControls":false,"controls":false,"showDistribution":false,"showSampleAxis":false,"highlightCurrent":false,"focus":"population"}' fallback="Interactive pathway from an IQ population through samples to a distribution of sample means." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="population" data-major-title="Population" data-title="Population" data-action='{"draw":0,"show-population":true,"observations":false,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":false,"show-distribution":false,"axis":true,"focus":"population","highlight-current":false,"show-controls":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":false,"fall-mean":false,"animate":false}'}
We start with the normally distributed IQ population, where $\mu=100$ and $\sigma=15$. As usual, this population is fixed; its characteristics don't change while we sample from it.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="one-sample" data-major-title="One sample" data-title="Select" data-action='{"draw":1,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":false,"axis":true,"focus":"sample","highlight-current":false,"show-controls":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":true,"fall-mean":false,"animate":true}'}
Now we select ten observations at random from the population.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="one-sample" data-major-title="One sample" data-title="Compute" data-action='{"draw":1,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":true,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":false,"axis":true,"focus":"mean","highlight-current":false,"show-controls":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":false,"fall-mean":false,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true}'}
Next we compute the sample mean: the balance point for this particular set of 10 observations. The <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">blue block marks this sample mean ($M =$ {{< interactive-value iqSamplingDistribution.currentMean format=".1f" >}})</span> on the sample's IQ-score axis.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="one-sample" data-major-title="One sample" data-title="Place mean" data-action='{"draw":1,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"distribution","highlight-current":false,"show-controls":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":false,"fall-mean":true,"delay":0,"animate":true}'}
We want to keep track of every sample mean we obtain, so now that <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">mean block</span> drops down onto the lower *Distribution of sample means* tracker. As we collect more means, this will become a kind of block histogram.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="two-samples" data-major-title="Two samples" data-title="Two samples" data-action='{"draw":2,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"sample-mean","highlight-current":false,"show-controls":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":false,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true}'}
Now we can take a second sample. It produces a <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">different mean block</span>, which drops down. The sample means are different even though the population hasn't changed. Each mean's difference from the population mean of 100 is that sample's sampling error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="thirty" data-major-title="Thirty samples" data-title="Thirty samples" data-action='{"draw":30,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"sample-mean","highlight-current":false,"show-controls":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":false,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true,"delay":440}'}
Now we just keep repeating the process. Each sample converges into a <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">blue mean block</span>, which joins the growing pile. After thirty samples, there isn't much of a pattern. But thirty isn't very many in the grand scheme of things: we need more.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="pattern" data-major-title="The pattern" data-title="The pattern" data-action='{"draw":200,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"sample-mean","highlight-current":false,"controls-open":false,"fall-observations":false,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":false,"animate":true,"delay":75}'}
Let's speed things up a bit. Each tick we get a new sample of 10 individual scores, from which we compute a new <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">sample mean</span>. After collecting 200 samples, a pattern is becoming evident. The distribution of means piles up around the true population mean in a roughly symmetrical distribution. Most sample means are near 100, and extreme ones are rare. The spread of the distribution of means is less than that of the original population.
:::
::::

:::::

Notice how similar the final shape of the histogram of sample means in @act-sampling-iq is to the shape of the balls at the bottom of the Quincunx. The process is different; instead of balls randomly bouncing off pegs, we are randomly selecting members of the population. But the reason for the outcome is similar: when we sample randomly from a population, there are lots of ways for a sample mean to be close to the true population mean, but few ways for it to be very far away.

The name for the kind of distribution we created is a __distribution of sample means__, or __sampling distribution of the mean__. And the predictability of its shape is the key insight that powers the inferential statistics we'll begin using in the next chapter. 

## The Distribution of Sample Means

Technically the sampling distribution of the mean is the distribution of sample means obtained by selecting *all possible samples of a given sample size $n$ from a population*. For the IQ distribution, we ended with 200 random samples, not *every* possible sample. As you might imagine, for any reasonably large population, there's often a huge number of possible samples; for practical purposes, the number might be effectively infinite. We'll return to this problem shortly, but we won't let it stop us from demonstrating the fundamental principles now. We just need a small, manageable population, from which we can obtain all possible samples of a given size. Like, very small.

Suppose we have a population consisting of just four people. We're interested in their height. We have one person 60 inches tall, one 62, one 64, and one 66.

| Height | $f$ |
|--:|--:|
| 60 | 1 |
| 62 | 1 |
| 64 | 1 |
| 66 | 1 |

: A frequency table showing the four heights in our population. There's just one person of each height. {#tbl-height-population}

We can describe some features of this population. Its mean is $\mu = 63$ inches^[$\mu = \frac{\Sigma X}{N} = \frac{60 + 62 + 64 + 66}{4} = 63$], and its standard deviation is $\sigma = 2.24$ inches.^[$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{(60-63)^2 + (62-63)^2 + (64-63)^2 + (66-63)^2}{4}} = \sqrt{\frac{9 + 1 + 1 + 9}{4}} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$.]

But remember, we're not interested in individuals anymore. We're interested in *samples*. So now we're going to list every possible sample where $n = 2$, meaning we have two observations in each sample. @tbl-height-samples lists every possible sample. $X_1$ is the first score in the sample. $X_2$ is the second score. And $M$ is that sample's mean. Note that for this to work, it is important that we're sampling independently, meaning that the first observation in each sample does not affect the second. For this tiny population that means the same person can appear twice. The first row, for example, is the 60-inch person twice. Obviously the sample mean there is 60. The next sample consists of the 62-inch person and the 60-inch person, giving a mean of 61. And so on.

| Sample | $X_1$ | $X_2$ | $M$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 60 | 60 | 60 |
| 2 | 62 | 60 | 61 |
| 3 | 64 | 60 | 62 |
| 4 | 66 | 60 | 63 |
| 5 | 60 | 62 | 61 |
| 6 | 62 | 62 | 62 |
| 7 | 64 | 62 | 63 |
| 8 | 66 | 62 | 64 |
| 9 | 60 | 64 | 62 |
| 10 | 62 | 64 | 63 |
| 11 | 64 | 64 | 64 |
| 12 | 66 | 64 | 65 |
| 13 | 60 | 66 | 63 |
| 14 | 62 | 66 | 64 |
| 15 | 64 | 66 | 65 |
| 16 | 66 | 66 | 66 |

: All 16 possible samples of $n = 2$ (with replacement) from the four heights. {#tbl-height-samples}

In case the tables don't make this process entirely clear, we can visualize the process of obtaining each sample and its mean step by step.

::::: {.callout-tip .interactive}
## Build every sample mean

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Population" data-action='{"draw":0,"show-population":true,"observations":false,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"none","show-controls":true,"controls-open":false,"highlight-current":false,"converge-mean":false,"animate":false}'}
The population is exactly four values, 60, 62, 64, and 66. If we plot them on a block histogram (well, technically a dot histogram in this case), it's pretty simple. Just four scores for the four different heights. The frequency of each is one because there's only one person of each height. So far, so simple.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sample 1" data-action='{"draw":1,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"none","show-controls":true,"controls-open":false,"highlight-current":false,"fall-observations":true,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true}'}
The first ordered sample is 60 and 60. Like with the IQ samples, we compute the sample mean and add a <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">mean block</span> to the distribution below.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sample 2" data-action='{"draw":2,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"none","show-controls":true,"controls-open":false,"highlight-current":false,"fall-observations":true,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true}'}
The next sample is 62 and 60, giving a <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">sample mean of 61</span>. The new mean block lands next to the first one down below.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sample 3" data-action='{"draw":3,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"none","show-controls":true,"controls-open":false,"highlight-current":false,"fall-observations":true,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true}'}
The third sample is 64 and 60, for a <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">sample mean of 62</span>.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="All 16" data-action='{"draw":16,"show-population":true,"observations":true,"show-mean":false,"show-sample-axis":true,"show-distribution":true,"axis":true,"focus":"none","show-controls":true,"controls-open":true,"highlight-current":false,"fall-observations":true,"fall-mean":true,"converge-mean":true,"animate":true,"delay":1200}'}
Now we just continue through the rest of the 16 possible samples. Each pair lands, we compute <span class="sfs-data-emphasis">the mean</span>, and add a block to the histogram below. After all 16 samples with replacement, the complete sampling distribution is visible.
:::
::::

:::::

So for this tiny population, we have been able to exhaustively compile every possible sample mean for samples of size $n = 2$---something we could only approximate with the bigger IQ population and the 200 means we collected randomly. But you see the similar pattern? Again, sample means close to the true population mean are relatively common; sample means far from the true population mean are relatively uncommon.

Now you might be wondering what the whole purpose of this quite tedious process was. Well, by going through the process of obtaining every possible sample mean, we now have the complete distribution of sample means, which is in fact a new kind of population: the population of every possible sample mean. And we can think about that population, and compute its characteristics, the same way we can with any other set of data.

We can, for example, figure out its mean. The mean of the distribution of sample means is __called the expected value of the mean__, $\mu_M$. Its value should be obvious visually. It's a symmetrical distribution and the peak is right on 63 inches, so that's the mean. You can also calculate it by adding all 16 sample means and dividing by 16, the number of scores. Remember, 63 was the mean of the population as well, so the mean of the sampling distribution is equal to $\mu$.

We can also calculate the standard deviation of the 16 means. The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is also called the __standard error of the mean__. The symbol for this is $\sigma_M$. We can calculate it in the same way we did in Chapter 4, by putting all those values in a table, working out columns for deviations, the squared deviations, then using those to get the sum of squared deviations, the variance, and the standard deviation. Note that because we're dealing with a population of sample means we use the population formula for variance, dividing $SS$ by $N$ (rather than $n - 1$ for a sample).

::: {#tbl-sampling-deviations}
{{< interactive-figure sampleMeansDeviationsTable makeVariabilityTable options='{"data":[60,61,62,63,61,62,63,64,62,63,64,65,63,64,65,66],"valueSymbol":"M","meanSymbol":"\\\\mu_M","varianceSymbol":"\\\\sigma_M^2","sdSymbol":"\\\\sigma_M","stage":"standard-deviation","controls":false}' fallback="Table of deviations and squared deviations for all 16 sample means, used to compute SS = 40, variance = 2.5, and standard deviation of about 1.58." >}}

Every sample mean, its deviation from the mean of the sampling distribution, and its squared deviation. The sum of squared deviations is 40, giving a variance of 2.50 and a standard error of about 1.58.
:::

Lastly, because we know every possible mean, we can think about the probability of observing certain sample means from this distribution, just like we thought about the probabilities of obtaining certain scores from a regular population.

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {#fig-sampling-prob-below-63}
{{< interactive-figure samplingProbBelow63 makeGraph options='{"type":"block","data":[60,61,62,63,61,62,63,64,62,63,64,65,63,64,65,66],"xDomain":[59,67],"xTickValues":[60,61,62,63,64,65,66],"colors":{"60":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)","61":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)","62":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)"},"labels":{"x":"Sample mean height (inches)","y":"Frequency"},"ariaLabel":"Block histogram of the 16 sample means, with the blocks at 60, 61, and 62 highlighted in orange."}' fallback="Block histogram of the 16 sample means, with the blocks below 63---means of 60, 61, and 62, six blocks in all---highlighted." >}}

The highlighted blocks are every sample mean below 63.
:::

$$ P(M < 63) = \frac{6}{16} = .375 $$
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {#fig-sampling-prob-extreme}
{{< interactive-figure samplingProbExtreme makeGraph options='{"type":"block","data":[60,61,62,63,61,62,63,64,62,63,64,65,63,64,65,66],"xDomain":[59,67],"xTickValues":[60,61,62,63,64,65,66],"colors":{"60":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)","66":"var(--graph-series-4, #d55e00)"},"labels":{"x":"Sample mean height (inches)","y":"Frequency"},"ariaLabel":"Block histogram of the 16 sample means, with the blocks at 60 and 66 highlighted in orange."}' fallback="Block histogram of the 16 sample means, with the two most extreme blocks, 60 and 66, highlighted." >}}

## The Central Limit Theorem

The trouble with distributions of sample means is that it's just not feasible in most realistic situations to obtain every possible sample of a given size for a population. We were able to do it with a population of just four people and samples of two. But imagine computing every possible sample of a given size from a population we'd actually be interested in, like, say, American voters. Even if we had the scores of everyone in the population, which we usually don't, the number of possible samples would be astronomical for any useful sample size. There would just be too many combinations.

Thankfully, there is a tool that allows us to predict the characteristics of the distribution of sample means without having to compile every possible sample. It is called the __Central Limit Theorem__.

We can predict the sampling distribution's center and variability from just the population mean, population variability, and sample size. The central limit theorem adds a prediction about shape; the center and variability formulas below hold without requiring normality.

### Center: The Expected Value of the Mean

Under the usual conditions—independent observations drawn in the same way from a population with a finite mean and variance—the average of all the sample means equals the population mean. This is because $M$ is an unbiased statistic: some of the sample means are above the true population mean, some are below, and they balance out perfectly. So the expected value of the mean is exactly equal to the population mean:

$$\mu_M = \mu$$ {#eq-expected-value}

Remember for our little toy population of four heights, we calculated the population mean as $\mu = 63$. And after listing all 16 possible samples of $n = 2$ for that population, we found that the mean of the sample means was also $\mu_M = 63$. It wasn't a coincidence! The central limit theorem tells us it will always be the case.

### Variability: The Standard Error of the Mean

As we demonstrated in Chapter 4, variability is also an unbiased statistic when it is computed appropriately. But unlike its center, the variability of the sampling distribution (its standard error, $\sigma_M$) is not equal to the population variability. Instead it is smaller, as a function of the sample size, $n$. 

$$\sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$ {#eq-s_m-1}

The numerator is the population standard deviation, $\sigma$. So the larger the variability in the population, the larger the standard error of the mean. The denominator is the square root of the sample size. And so the larger our sample size, the smaller the standard error of the mean.

An algebraically equivalent form is useful if you have variance, $\sigma^2$, rather than the standard deviation, $\sigma$:

$$\sigma_M = \dfrac{\sqrt{\sigma^2}}{\sqrt{n}}$$ {#eq-s_m-2}

You can see how they are equivalent: $\sigma^2$ is literally just $\sigma$ squared, so $\sqrt{\sigma^2}$ is the same as $\sigma$.

Returning to our toy population of heights, we can figure out the standard error of the mean using just known population characteristics. Remember, we said the standard deviation of the population of four heights is $\sigma = 2.24$. So if we put it into that equation, we get:

$$\sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{2.24}{\sqrt{2}} = 1.58$$

It's the same answer as when we went through the full rigmarole of compiling all possible samples for that little population and computing their standard deviation manually! Plugging two numbers into an equation could have saved us a lot of work there.

Of course, the real value is that we can apply this equation in situations where we couldn't compile all possible samples to double-check the answer. Applying this to the IQ distribution that we sampled from earlier, we can see how the standard error of the mean changes as a function of sample size. Since $n$ is in the denominator of the equation, as $n$ increases, the standard error decreases.

### Shape of the Sampling Distribution

It wasn't a coincidence that the distribution of the Quincunx balls, IQ samples, and height sampling distribution all took on the same basic shape: symmetrical, bell-shaped, and unimodal. The Central Limit Theorem tells us that this is a general property of sampling distributions of the mean. Under suitable conditions, the distribution of sample means will be approximately normal, even if the population itself is not normally distributed.

As we pointed out along the way, the balls' devious courses and the sample means are affected by randomness. But as long as the randomness is unbiased, unusually extreme values below the average are balanced by unusually extreme values above the average, and both extremes are proportionally rare compared to values near the average. The result is the normal distribution.

What exactly are the *suitable conditions* though? For one, if the population is normally distributed, its distribution of sample means will be exactly normal at every sample size. But even if the population is not normal, the distribution of sample means will still become progressively more normal as the sample size increases. The larger the sample size, the closer the distribution of means will be to normal.

There's no mathematical threshold or magic sample size at which the distribution of means suddenly becomes normal. In fact, the distribution of means will never be *exactly* normal for a nonnormal population, no matter how large the sample size. But there does come a point at which it's close enough that the difference is negligible for practical purposes. You will sometimes hear $n = 30$ as a rule of thumb for when the distribution of means is "close enough" to normal. But that is just a rough guideline, not an absolute. The convergence is gradual, and the rate of convergence depends on how nonnormal the population is. The more nonnormal the population, the larger the sample size needed for the distribution of means to be approximately normal. @act-clt-normality lets us see that distinction in action.

::::: {#act-clt-normality .callout-tip .interactive}

Here come a million independent samples of $n=5$. Averaging five observations makes the distribution of means less skewed than the population, but the histogram still doesn't quite match the perfectly normal curve. The peak sits a little left of the prediction, and the right tail extends farther.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Samples of 30" data-action='{"distribution":"skewed","n":30,"samples":1000000,"sampling-duration":4000,"scale":"raw","show-ruler":false,"show-population":true,"show-distribution":true,"show-normal":true,"controls-open":false,"animate":true}' }
Now we'll keep the same skewed population, but increase each sample to $n=30$ and generate one million new means. The distribution is narrower again, and now looks much closer to normal. But it's still not quite perfectly normal.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Add a ruler" data-action='{"distribution":"skewed","n":30,"samples":1000000,"scale":"raw","show-ruler":true,"show-population":true,"show-distribution":true,"show-normal":true,"controls-open":false,"animate":true}' }
The difference between the normal curve and the actual distribution is hard to see at this scale, so we can zoom in (without reshaping the data). First I'll add a second ruler underneath the scores, like we did in Chapter 5. Its center is $\mu$, and each unit is one standard error, $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Stretch the ruler" data-action='{"distribution":"skewed","n":30,"samples":1000000,"scale":"se","show-ruler":true,"show-population":true,"show-distribution":true,"show-normal":true,"controls-open":true,"animate":true}' }
Now we can stretch the distribution to fill the lower panel, again just changing the scale, not the actual data. The histogram and predicted curve stretch with it, keeping the same values lined up. These are still the same one million means. This allows us to see better that a little asymmetry remains. So increasing sample size to $n=30$ hasn't flipped a switch that makes the distribution exactly normal.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Samples of 100" data-action='{"distribution":"skewed","n":100,"samples":1000000,"sampling-duration":4000,"scale":"se","show-ruler":true,"show-population":true,"show-distribution":true,"show-normal":true,"controls-open":true,"animate":true}' }
Now let's increase sample size again, to $n=100$, and generate one million new means. We'll keep the standard-error ruler stretched out so we can compare the shapes more easily. The histogram follows the normal curve even more closely than at $n = 30$, but the distribution of means still isn't perfectly normal. The improvement is gradual, with no special boundary at 30 or anywhere else. The approximation may be good enough, but how much remaining nonnormality matters depends on what we use it for.
:::

## Sampling People in Practice

So now we've seen a few examples of normality and predictability emerging from random sampling. We're almost ready to apply these tools in the context of social science research. But first, let's take a moment to consider how closely collecting data from people resembles the sampling in our demonstrations. The version of the Central Limit Theorem we've used assumes independent observations drawn from the same population distribution; applying it in practice requires those assumptions to be reasonable approximations.

### Random Selection, Replacement, and Independence

First let's define three terms. **Random sampling** is about how we choose observations: we use a chance procedure. **Replacement** is about whether someone or something already selected can be selected again within the same sample. **Independence** is about whether knowing one observation changes the probabilities for another.

In the demonstrations above, I sampled with replacement. This was most obvious with the small population of four heights: the 16 possible samples of $n = 2$ included samples in which the same person appeared twice. To see why that mattered, let's turn to another statistics textbook favorite: picking marbles out of a jar.

In *The Art of Conjecturing*, published in 1713, Jacob Bernoulli asked his reader to imagine an urn containing 5,000 pebbles, in some unknown ratio of white to black. By drawing pebbles repeatedly, someone who couldn't see the contents could estimate that ratio from the proportion of white pebbles they observed [@bernoulli2006conjecturing].

To keep things simple, imagine a jar with just 50 marbles, 40 blue and 10 white. We want to pick out two marbles, one after the other. If each marble is equally likely to be drawn, the probability of white on our first draw is $P(\text{white})=10/50=.2$.

So far so simple. But what is the probability that a second draw will also be white? To answer that, we need to know a small but important procedural detail: did we put the first marble back, or leave it out?

If we **sample with replacement**, we put it back and mix the jar before drawing again. There are still 10 white marbles among 50, so the probability stays .2, whatever color we drew first. The draws are independent.

If we **sample without replacement**, we leave the first marble out. After drawing white, only 9 white marbles and 49 marbles in total remain, so the probability of another white is $9/49 \approx .184$. After drawing blue, it would instead be $10/49 \approx .204$. The draws are dependent: knowing the first result changes the probabilities for the second.

Both procedures are random, but only the first gives us independent draws. For people, choosing names by lottery from a complete population list works the same way. Without replacement, this produces a **simple random sample**: every possible set of $n$ people has the same chance of being selected. Random doesn't mean choosing whoever happens to be nearby, and it doesn't require replacement.

### Can We Treat People's Scores as Independent?

Do you sense a potential problem here? Social scientists generally aren't sampling marbles from a jar, or dots from a simulated digital distribution. We're interested in *people*: we want to see what they get up to, ask them questions, measure their physiological responses, or whatever. And people are not like marbles that we can easily put back into a jar.

Social scientists generally collect data from each participant once, so they sample without replacement. Strictly speaking, this makes successive selections dependent. But like the (non)normality of the sampling distribution, the problem is a matter of degree. What matters is the fraction sampled across the *whole sample*, not just the tiny change after the first draw. If the sample is only a small fraction of the population, removing those people barely changes who is available. Selecting 100 people randomly from a population of 10,000 removes just 1% of the population in total. For the sampling distribution of the mean, the resulting dependence is small enough that the independent-draw model is a useful approximation. If we sampled most of those 10,000 people, sampling without replacement would noticeably reduce the variability of the mean, and $\sigma_M=\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ would overstate the standard error.^[There are methods for adjusting for this, but that's beyond the scope of this book.]

Still, would allowing someone to participate twice be a better idea? Usually not. In our toy height example, independently drawing a person, replacing them, and drawing again gives independent draws of the recorded heights, even if the same person comes up twice. But participating in a study can change a person: they may learn the task, remember the questions, or guess what we're testing. Even if we independently select them again, we can't make them naive to the procedure again. (Sometimes this is precisely what we want though: for example, if we want to measure the effect of a treatment, we might want to measure the same person before and after the treatment. Deliberately measuring each person twice raises a separate issue: the paired responses are related, so we need an analysis that accounts for that.)

Dependence can also arise among different people. Responses from members of one household may share influences; pupils in one classroom share a teacher and learning environment. An opinion poll sampling whole households could underestimate the standard error if it treated all their responses as independent. Studies that do things like that can still be useful, but their analysis needs to account for dependence.

### Which Population Are We Sampling?

Lastly, we should point out that even if we are appropriately ensuring independence in a statistical sense, we still need to be careful that our sample is a fair representation of the population we are trying to make inferences about. Remember Köbel's proposal in Chapter 3 to define a foot by averaging the feet of sixteen men leaving church? Suppose we wanted to estimate the average foot length of the town's adult men. A simple random sample could happen to include some unusually large feet. That's sampling error; across repeated random samples, high and low estimates would balance around those men's mean.

Now imagine trying Köbel's procedure outside the locker room of the New York Knicks basketball team. We'd probably get a much larger average foot size. Or imagine lining up my kid's second-grade class: we'd get a much smaller answer. Both procedures systematically favor feet unlike those of the town's complete population of adult men: that's **selection bias**. Even choosing randomly within those niche groups of basketball players or kids wouldn't fix it.

Somewhat more subtly, say we recruit people for an opinion poll by randomly dialing phone numbers listed in a database. People who answer and agree to tell us their thoughts may differ from those who don't, and not everyone in the population might have a number in our database. Those are coverage and nonresponse problems. Alternatively, recruiting whoever walks past, volunteers online, or participates for course credit gives us a **convenience sample**, rather than a simple random sample of the general population. (Arguably Köbel's churchgoers were a convenience sample; the men who attended church might not represent the broader population.)

Convenience sampling can be perfectly acceptable for some research questions, and the Central Limit Theorem still applies if treating its scores as independent observations from a common population distribution is reasonable and the sample is large enough. But generalizing beyond the population we actually sampled needs a separate argument, and increasing the sample size can't fix a procedure that systematically produces biased data.

{{< include quizzes/07-sampling-random-sampling-checks.qmd >}}

## Summary

So to repeat and summarize, assuming we are independently sampling from a population, the distribution of sample means has an expected value, $\mu_M$, equal to $\mu$. It has a standard deviation, or standard error of the mean, of $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$. Its shape is exactly normal at every $n$ when the population is normal. For a nonnormal population, its standardized shape approaches normality gradually as $n$ increases, at a rate that depends on the skew in the population. $n = 30$ is often a useful convention, but it is not a magical cutoff. And we need to design our recruitment and sampling procedures carefully to ensure that the assumptions of independence and random sampling are met, and that we are sampling from a population that is representative of the group we want to make inferences about. These insights power much of the inferential statistics that we'll move on to later, because they allow us to reason about the probability of sample statistics rather than only individual scores.
